items.title: Build-to-rent communities now eligible for FHA financing
items.description: Politics and policy Build-to-rent communities now eligible for FHA financing By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published October 15, 2026, 4:56 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Processing Content What's at Stake: Whether the new FHA financing will actually lower rents or expand housing supply. Expert Quote: "It does not alter real-world bottlenecks" — Thom Malone, principal economist, Cotality Supporting Data: Fewer than 100,000 annual starts for one specific property type. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Build-to-rent lending, a property type exempted from the ownership restrictions in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, got a boost from the Department of Housing and Urban Development on Wednesday. If anything, the Act was expected to create a shift among business-purpose lenders away from single-family rental transactions towards BTR properties. Some BPL originators acquire their production through the correspondent channel. These properties are now eligible for Federal Housing Administration-insurance under two multifamily programs: Section 221(d)(4) for new construction and Section 223(f) for acquisition or refinancing of recently developed rental communities. "In theory, this announcement will lower the cost of capital for BTR by providing more stable and cheaper financing options," said Thom Malone, principal economist for Cotality. "This would increase the supply of rental housing, which would put downward pressure on rents, but that would be blunted since it would also increase demand by making more families choose renting over buying." However, Malone thinks the effects would be extremely small, possibly not even detectable in practice. "Even if the cost of capital is lower, it does not alter real-world bottlenecks like processing delays and restrictive local zoning," Malone continued. BTR is not a large part of the market, he said, with the number of starts totalling fewer than 100,000 a year. "Even if this program increased that by 20%, that would still mean only 15,000 to 20,000 more rental units — a drop in the bucket of the U.S. rental market," Malone said. Still, this change not only helps those who need this type of financing but also gives lenders another product they can offer at a time when industry economists are expecting owner-occupied residential volume to decline 5% in 2027. HUD Secretary Scott Turner. Photographer: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg "America needs more affordable housing," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release. "We're eliminating barriers to spur development, expand rental options and improve housing affordability for hardworking American families." While a fair amount of investor-property loans goes through the non-agency market, certain non-owner occupied premises are eligible for government-sponsored enterprise financing. The Community Home Lenders of America, whose membership consists of single-family originators who concentrate on the owner-occupied segment, still sees this announcement as having a broader impact on housing. "We need an 'all hands on deck' approach to our nation's affordable housing challenges," Scott Olson, the group's executive director, said. "So while this does not directly affect homeownership — CHLA's top priority as the trade group exclusively representing non-bank single-family lenders — housing is a continuum, and this is a very constructive action, which CHLA supports, to develop more affordable rental housing." Build-to-rent communities typically consist of single-family homes, duplexes or triplexes. Under the change, FHA insurance will cover both site-built and manufactured home BTRs and treat them under the same terms and conditions as traditional multifamily rental developments. items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Las Vegas multifamily market report here.HighlightsLas Vegas multifamily operating conditions remain soft, with elevated vacancy, rising concessions and declining rents. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, but the improved supply-demand balance has yet to translate into rent growth.Stabilized vacancy reached 9.1% at the end of the third quarter, flat from the prior quarter but up 20 basis points from one year earlier. Vacancy remains 30 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month by the end of September, down 1.4% year over year and 0.9% lower than in the prior quarter, the second consecutive quarterly decline.Investment sales volume during the third quarter totaled roughly $209 million across five deals, with Class B properties accounting for four of the five deals. The year-to-date median sale price reached $225,900 per unit.Las Vegas multifamily market overviewLas Vegas multifamily fundamentals remain under pressure despite improved absorption and a slowdown in new deliveries in 2026. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries by roughly 650 units year to date, after trailing them by nearly 1,700 units in 2025. Absorption has already surpassed the full-year 2025 total, supported by continued job growth, while completions have slowed as fewer projects remain under construction. The recovery has been concentrated in the suburbs, where Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of that demand with less than half of the metro’s inventory. Rent growth has been slower to rebound. Asking rents remain below year-ago levels, with the steepest declines in older urban core submarkets, where vacancy is above 10%. By contrast, rents in suburban submarkets remain close to year-ago levels.Investment activity in 2026 has become concentrated in two of the suburban submarkets that are leading the leasing recovery. Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson accounted for roughly three-quarters of metro sales volume through the third quarter, up from 43% in 2025. Third-quarter activity followed the same pattern, with three of the five trades located in those two submarkets. Pricing has remained stable in Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson, with median sale prices near $250,000 per unit in both submarkets, above levels elsewhere in the metro, where recent trades have skewed toward smaller, older properties. The median price across the Las Vegas region has remained near its 2025 level, highlighting the influence of property location on pricing trends.Employment:Area employers added 21,400 jobs year over year. Year-to-date deliveries total around 2,600 units, down 23% from the same period in 2025. Roughly 6,100 units were under construction at the end of the third quarter, down more than 25% from the end of 2025, which is expected to ease supply pressure on operators heading into 2027. Six active projects in Spring Valley total more than 2,000 units.Multifamily permitting activity is regaining momentum. Developers pulled permits for 1,130 multifamily units in the third quarter, more than double the total from one year earlier.Forecast: Developers are expected to complete roughly 4,000 units in 2026, in line with both the 2025 total and the 10-year average.Vacancy:Vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1% Image Stabilized vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1%, up 20 basis points year over year. Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of net absorption this year, each with vacancy below 7.5%. items.description: Share: Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn I recommend visiting cushmanwakefield.com to read:%0A%0A {0} %0A%0A {1} Insights U.S. Industrial Reports With logistics playing a critical role in business strategy, understanding the industrial market is essential. DOWNLOAD Q3 2026 REPORT Key INDUSTRIAL Takeaways For Q3 2026 Quarterly net absorption reached 76.6 million square feet (msf), its highest level since Q1 2023. Demand surpassed 70 msf for the second consecutive quarter, bringing the year-to-date (YTD) total to 203 msf, the strongest three-quarter stretch since late 2022. New industrial supply remained modest in Q3 2026, with 64 msf delivered nationwide. Completions YTD are 13% behind last year's pace. The national industrial vacancy rate fell 20 basis points (bps) from year-end 2025 to 6.8%, its lowest level since year-end 2024. Developer confidence is returning as demand strengthens and vacancy stabilizes. The under-construction pipeline increased 23% year-over-year (YOY) to 324 msf, its highest level since mid-2024. For the data behind the commentary, download the full Q3 2026 U.S. Industrial Report. Despite Economic Uncertainties, Industrial Demand Accelerates Net absorption accelerated to 76.6 msf in Q3, its strongest quarter since Q1 2023. Demand exceeded 70 msf for a second consecutive quarter, lifting the YTD total to 203 msf, 69% higher than the first three quarters of 2025. Inland markets are driving activity, accounting for 80% of YTD absorption. Port markets are also improving, with YTD demand already surpassing the full-year 2025 total, led by third-quarter surges in Houston, New Jersey, the Inland Empire, Savannah and Miami. Newer product continues to attract the strongest demand, with 202 msf of YTD net absorption in warehouses built this decade. However, as availability in newer facilities tightens, demand is beginning to spill over into older properties. Warehouses built from 2000 through 2019, which experienced steady occupancy losses over the previous two years, are now showing signs of stabilization. New leasing YTD is 21% above last year's pace. The surge in AI buildouts, resilient consumer spending, and nearshoring and onshoring has propelled leasing activity to its strongest six-month period in more than four years. Demand has been led by 3PL, manufacturing, e-commerce and data center-related tenants. Manufacturers remained the second most active tenant type through the first three quarters of 2026 as they continue to build out and evolve their supply chains nationwide. After accounting for 23% of annual leasing volume the previous three years, manufacturing companies represented more than one-fourth of YTD 2026 activity. Tenants looking for large format warehouses have been particularly active, with transactions above 500,000 sf making up more than one-third of YTD leasing volume. Nationwide Vacancy Drifts Further Below Its Recent Peak With demand outpacing new supply for two straight quarters, U.S. industrial vacancy has fallen 20 bps from its late-2025 peak of 7%. At 6.8%, the rate is at its lowest point since year-end 2024 and is expected to decline modestly by the end of 2026. Vacancy fell by 100 bps or more YOY in 14 U.S. markets, including Indianapolis, Columbus, Phoenix, Central Valley and Philadelphia. Larger facilities have led the compression. Vacancy in buildings of 500,000 sf or more fell 280 bps YOY to 7.4%, while the mid-sized segment (300,000--500,000 sf) is also stabilizing, with vacancy down 50 bps. Asking rental rate growth reached 4% nationwide in Q3, up from roughly 1% during the second half of 2025 and marking the third consecutive quarter of acceleration. Strong gains in the South and Midwest contributed. Of the 83 markets tracked, 13 reported double-digit YOY growth in Q3, led by Dallas-Fort Worth at 20%. St. Louis, Louisville, Tampa, Raleigh-Durham and Indianapolis all posted annual rent growth above 10%. Conversely, rents continued to soften in some key coastal markets in California, New Jersey and Miami. New Deliveries Remain Modest, But the Pipeline Is Expanding New supply remained modest, with nearly 64 msf of completions in Q3. The YTD total of 185 msf is down 13% YOY. Texas accounted for one-fourth of U.S. deliveries in 2026 (47 msf), while five other inland markets each recorded more than 5 msf of completions: the PA I-81/I-78 Corridor, Chicago, Atlanta, Phoenix and Louisville. In some smaller markets, including El Paso, Fredericksburg, Boise and Raleigh-Durham, YTD completions equal more than 3% of their current inventories. As leasing activity strengthens and vacancy stabilizes, developers are growing more confident. The pipeline rose 23% YOY to 324 msf, its highest level since mid-2024. Pipelines grew YOY in half of U.S. markets, including 14 with gains of more than 100%. Build-to-suit projects make up about 35% of the overall pipeline and more than 55% of the large-format pipeline (500,000 sf or more), as large logistics tenants seek customized facilities for long-term needs. items.title: Fundamentals Take the Lead as Capital Stays Selective
items.description: Fundamentals Take the Lead as Capital Stays Selective Oct 21, 2026 | 5 min read U.S. Capital Markets Snapshot Report | Q3 2026 Property fundamentals continued to improve during the third quarter even as capital remained selective. Download Report Experts David Amsterdam President, Capital Markets | U.S. David Goodhue Executive Managing Director | Boston & Head of Multifamily Capital Markets | U.S Rachael Rothman Director, National Capital Markets Research Share Article Key Themes Improving property fundamentals are increasingly driving investment decisions. Capital remains selective, favoring assets with durable cash flow and limited competition. Distress continues to create opportunities, particularly within the office sector. Slowing development activity is supporting long-term occupancy and rent growth across several sectors. Multifamily: Recovery Becomes Increasingly Regional Multifamily is entering a more favorable phase as construction pipelines continue to contract and supply pressures ease. However, performance is becoming increasingly market-specific, with West Coast asking rents rising 3.2% year over year while several East Coast and Sun Belt markets continue to work through elevated supply levels. Office: Distress Creates Opportunity Office investment activity continues to gain traction in select markets as improving leasing conditions and deeply reset values attract capital. Demand remains concentrated in trophy and well-located properties, while elevated distress and refinancing pressure continue to create recapitalization, restructuring, and acquisition opportunities across the sector. Industrial: Liquidity Remains Strong Industrial remains one of the most liquid and institutionally favored asset classes. Sales volume reached its highest Q1-Q3 level since 2022, while durable occupier demand and a slowing development pipeline continue to support investor interest. Retail: Supply-Demand Fundamentals Remain Strong Retail continues to benefit from limited new supply, healthy occupancy, and steady consumer demand. Grocery-anchored and necessity-based formats remain highly sought after, supported by durable cash flows and a retail environment increasingly shaped by omnichannel shopping strategies. Hospitality: Operating Fundamentals Continue to Improve Hospitality investment activity is strengthening as limited new construction supports operating performance. RevPAR growth rebounded in September as demand strengthened across the market, supported by group travel and continued domestic demand. Questions This Report Answers Q: What are the current cap rates for core commercial real estate sectors? A: As of Q3 2026, core cap rates are 5.4% for multifamily, 7.4% for office, 5.1% for industrial, 6.6% for malls and 6.3% for strip centers within the retail sector, and 8.5% for hospitality, reflecting continued variation in pricing and investor sentiment across major property sectors. Q: How is the multifamily recovery evolving across U.S. markets? A: The development pipeline continues to shrink, reducing future supply pressures. At the same time, performance is diverging by region, with West Coast markets outperforming many East Coast and Sun Belt markets. Q: What is driving investment activity in the office sector despite elevated distress? A: Improving leasing activity, limited new supply, and deeply reset property values are creating opportunities for buyers focused on high-quality assets and value-add repositioning strategies. Q: Why does industrial remain a preferred allocation for institutional capital? A: Durable tenant demand, sustained transaction volume, slowing supply growth, and confidence in long-term demand drivers continue to make industrial one of the most attractive sectors for institutional investors. Q: How are investors approaching the retail sector in an omnichannel environment? A: Investors remain focused on grocery-anchored and necessity-based formats that complement evolving consumer shopping behaviors while providing stable cash flow and limited competitive supply. items.title: The Rate Path Wildcard (October 2026 Housing Market Forecast)
items.description: The Rate Path Wildcard (October 2026 Housing Market Forecast) Written by Mischa Fisher on October 23, 2026 The decline in existing home sales is forecasted to accelerate in the fourth quarter, as our moving average of newly pending existing home sales dropped 12.8% in Zillow's latest weekly data. Total annual sales are still forecasted to finish up slightly in 2026 relative to 2025, given the lower share of sales volume the fourth quarter contributes. Inventory growth is expected to increase 6.6% Y/Y in Q4, alongside home value growth of only 0.7% Rent growth is continuing to build, with rents expected to grow 2.4% in multifamily and 3.2% in single-family in the fourth quarter. Given the volatility in mortgage rate paths, mathematical models are more likely to require revision. As we’ve continued to note in a variety of commentary : the current economic cycle is a strange one. We’ve added a rate hiking cycle with its expected contractionary effects on top of a weak housing market rather than on top of a strong market, defying the normal story we expected from Ed Leamer’s characterization that housing is the business cycle. As a result we’re expecting October existing home sales (we’ll release full month statistics on November 5th ) to be down considerably year-over-year. (On a rolling average weekly basis, newly pending listings dropped a whopping 12.8% year-over-year in our latest weekly data ). But the most important question right now for both housing and the economy is what else is slowed by high interest rates, and how soon. If the past is prologue we expect at some point a return to more normal market dynamics, where housing leads the business cycle. This necessarily means something else in the economy would need to slow first, the question is when. For example, we’ve seen recent selloffs in the AI related equity market paired with some nervousness about expectations for return on invested capital. So if this or another part of the economy outside of housing does indeed slow, then we’d expect investors to migrate to the safety of longer dated securities, mortgage rates to come down, home sales to rise, and housing to lead the business cycle again. But while there are early signs of this, it hasn’t happened yet. So while our current outlook is based on the current rate path, I think it’s increasingly likely that the actual path we follow will either be notably better or worse than what the math would predict. (Worse, if inflation isn’t brought under control, or better if inflation and/or growth expectations drop sooner rather than later). With that caveat on the current math noted, here’s what our latest forecast predicts. items.title: Select Markets Drive U.S. Office Market Recovery
items.description: Select Markets Drive U.S. Office Market Recovery Oct 29, 2026 U.S. Office Market Outlook Report | Q3 2026 Download Report Experts Marianne Skorupski Director, National Office Research Matthew Gannon Executive Managing Director | Washington D.C. & Head of Agency Leasing | U.S. Jodie Poirier President, Occupier Services & Agency Leasing Market Summary The U.S. office market strengthened in Q3 2026, with the national vacancy rate declining to 17.7%, down 60 basis points from one year ago and the lowest level since Q4 2023. Positive net absorption continued for a ninth consecutive quarter, while demand remained concentrated in high-quality Class A and trophy office buildings across major markets, including New York, San Francisco, Boston, and Seattle. Limited development activity and declining sublease availability are supporting occupancy and rent growth in top-performing assets. items.title: Texas Housing Insight | October 2026 | Texas Real Estate Research Center
items.description: Texas Housing Insight | October 2026 Texas housing activity slowed in August as higher mortgage rates and affordability pressures dampened demand. Inventory remains elevated, prices are stabilizing, and sales may weaken further as rates above 7 percent continue to challenge buyers and sellers. By Yanling Mayer quick links Texas housing market activity slowed in August as the market moved beyond the peak summer selling season and mortgage rates trended higher. Rising Treasury yields and rising inflation pushed mortgage rates upward during the month, impacting buyers already confronting affordability issues. While August's pullback also reflects a typical seasonal cooling, higher financing costs likely amplified the slowdown. Year to date (YTD), sales remain modestly ahead of last year’s, but the lead is expected to narrow in the coming months as mortgage rates have climbed further since August. Statewide, new listing activity largely tracked last year's pace through August, suggesting that homeowners remain willing to enter the market despite slower sales. However, conditions vary across major metropolitan areas. DFW stands out as the weakest large market on the supply side, with new listing volumes remaining soft since April and YTD activity trailing last year's levels. In contrast, seller participation in Austin, Houston, and San Antonio has remained comparatively stable. Active inventory, which expanded steadily throughout the spring and summer, began its normal seasonal decline in August. Even so, inventory levels remain broadly stable and elevated. While some buyers may have been able to take advantage of inventory availability and large seller price concessions, ongoing affordability challenges continue to limit many buyers from fully benefiting from these conditions. Meanwhile, measures such as days on market and inventory turnover suggest that the pace of sales activity remained broadly similar to that of a year ago. Price trends continue to show encouraging signs of stabilization. After more than a year of modest annual declines, statewide home prices were essentially flat in August, breaking a 15-month streak of downward pressures. The moderation in price declines reflects a market that is gradually finding better footing as inventory conditions normalize. Conditions remain somewhat uneven across metros, but overall pricing trends suggest easing downward pricing pressures. Prices in Houston and Fort Worth have trended slightly higher in recent months. Looking ahead, housing activity is likely to remain restrained and could slow further through the remainder of the year. Mortgage rates have climbed back above 7 percent, a threshold that previously weighed heavily on buyers and sellers during the 2023 market downturn. September inflation data suggests overall cost-of-living price pressures remain persistent and rising, raising concerns that interest rates may stay elevated for longer. That means affordability challenges are likely to intensify, creating additional headwinds for home sales and overall housing market activity. On a YTD basis, sales remain ahead of last year’s pace in Austin (+7.8 percent), San Antonio (+1.6 percent), and DFW (+0.9 percent), while Houston trails (-1.2 percent). Invitation Homes Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results
Dallas, TX, October 28, 2026 — Invitation Homes Inc. (NYSE: INVH) (“Invitation Homes,” “we,” “our,” and “us”), the nation’s

Q3 2026 Highlights

U.S. home values fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August's 3.4% inflation ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the 2.1% home price gain. NEW YORK , Oct. 27, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P DJI) today released the August 2026 results for the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Indices. More than 27 years of history are available for the data series and can be accessed in full by going to www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/index-family/indicators/sp-Cotality-case-shiller . The divergence suggests that the typical post-summer slowdown is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices. "Affordability, however, remains challenging. With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices." items.description: Industrial Market Real Estate Trends U.S. Industrial Market Outlook – September 2026 Diana Firtea October 5, 2026 2 Min Read Image by Roman Vyshnikov/iStock Industrial fundamentals continued to rebalance in August, while renewed construction activity and record e-commerce penetration pointed to durable long-term logistics demand, the latest Yardi Matrix Industrial National Report shows. Report highlights In-place rents averaged $9.31 per square foot, up 5.4 percent year over year National vacancy held at 9.3 percent, up 60 basis points annually Leases signed during the past 12 months averaged $10.19 per square foot 446.9 million square feet of industrial space was under construction, equal to 2.1 percent of stock Industrial sales totaled $60.5 billion through August at $138 per square foot Leasing conditions remain uneven Rent growth remained strongest in several Sun Belt and East Coast markets. Atlanta led major metros with a 7.9 percent annual increase, followed by New Jersey and Miami at 7.6 percent and Dallas at 7.5 percent. Higher-priced coastal markets included Orange County at $18.09 per square foot, Los Angeles at $15.97 and the Bay Area at $15.29. The national spread between new and in-place leases continued to compress. Newly signed leases averaged $10.19 per square foot, just $0.88 above the $9.31 in-place average. Bridgeport retained the widest premium at $3.52, followed by Boston at $3.02 and Miami at $2.97. Seattle moved in the opposite direction of the strongest rent-growth markets. Its vacancy rate reached 13.6 percent after rising 500 basis points in two years, reflecting the absorption challenge created by 44.2 million square feet delivered since the start of 2020. Large projects reshape the pipeline Industrial construction reached 446.9 million square feet nationally. Dallas led in absolute volume with 37.3 million square feet underway, followed by Phoenix with 31.1 million and Houston with 21.8 million. Phoenix had the largest pipeline relative to existing inventory at 6.8 percent of stock, with another 7.2 percent planned. Large-format development is becoming increasingly important. Forty-nine projects exceeding 1 million square feet broke ground through August, and facilities of that scale accounted for more than 32 percent of all 2026 starts by square footage. Demand is also receiving support from e-commerce, which reached a record 20.2 percent of core retail sales in the second quarter. Meanwhile, industrial transactions totaled $60.5 billion through August. Dallas recorded the most sales at $4.1 billion, while Los Angeles averaged $297 per square foot and Memphis averaged $75, illustrating the wide dispersion in pricing nationally. Demand Is Running at Its Strongest Pace Since 2021 National vacancy fell 30 bps QOQ to 8.6% in Q3, hitting the lowest reading since Q3 2023 after three consecutive quarterly declines. Although vacancy remains roughly 140 bps above the long-run trend, the sustained improvement points to a multifamily market firmly in recovery. Strong demand is the clear driver. YTD absorption reached nearly 350,000 units, 14% above the same period last year and the strongest first three quarters of any year except 2021. A resilient economy continues to support household formation and renter demand, while higher interest rates and elevated home prices have widened the affordability gap between renting and owning. Texas continues to lead the demand recovery, with three of its markets among the nation's top five for absorption. Dallas/Ft. Worth leads with more than 50,000 units this year, followed by New York (37,000), Austin (34,000), Phoenix (31,000) and Houston (26,000 units). On a percentage basis, Sarasota (6.7% of inventory), Savannah (5.3%) and Boise (5.1%) saw the largest YTD increases. Supply-heavy markets such as Charlotte (4.4%) and Denver (3.7%) also rank in the top 20 as new lease-ups fill. New Supply Keeps Shrinking Deliveries totaled roughly 250,000 units through the first three quarters of 2026, down 25% from 335,000 units in the same period of 2025 and the lowest YTD total since 2021. The supply pipeline is set to slow further, with fewer than 480,000 units underway, the lowest level on a nominal basis since 2015. As a share of existing inventory, the construction pipeline stands at just 3.6%, the lowest since 2013 and less than half its recent peak. The pullback in construction activity is broad-based. More than 70% of the 90 markets tracked by Cushman & Wakefield Research have smaller construction pipelines than a year ago. The steepest declines came in the markets that built most aggressively during the boom. Sarasota's pipeline fell 790 bps as a share of inventory, while Savannah (-240 bps), Austin (-220 bps), Phoenix (-200 bps) and Salt Lake City (-200 bps) also recorded significant declines. Several Midwest markets pulled back sharply as well, led by Columbus (-330 bps) and Madison (-310 bps). Pipelines expanded in just 25 markets, most notably Palm Beach and the Bay Area, where stronger rent growth has improved developer economics. Rent Growth Accelerates as Occupancy Improves National asking rents rose 2.3% YOY to $1,950 in Q3, the fastest annual pace since Q1 2023 but roughly half the pre-pandemic average. Annual growth has more than doubled from its 1.1% trough in Q1 2026 as demand strengthened, and absorption outpaced deliveries in every quarter this year. Favorable base effects also contributed, as rents softened in the second half of 2025. The rent recovery is spreading beyond the Northeast and Midwest, which have led the nation since 2023. The West has seen the sharpest turnaround, with rent growth climbing from 0.6% at the end of 2025 to 2.6% in Q3, its strongest pace since late 2022. The Bay Area is driving much of that gain. San Francisco leads the nation at nearly 16% YOY growth, followed by San Jose (9%) and the East Bay (6.9%), as AI-related investment and job growth support renewed renter demand and greater landlord pricing power. Outside the Bay Area, rent growth across the West averaged a more modest 1.9%. The South is following the same path from a weaker starting point, with rent growth turning positive in Q2 and reaching 1.1% in Q3, its strongest reading since early 2025. The Northeast still leads at 3.7%, while the Midwest has slowed to 3% from above 4% between mid-2023 and early 2025, as several of the region's 17 markets saw vacancy rise over the past year. items.description: Pending Home Sales Decreased 7.3% in September Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More October 20, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Financing & Credit , Mortgages & Home Financing Share View and share this infographic Month-Over-Month 7.3% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions Year-Over-Year 11.3% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions View Pending Home Sales Report WASHINGTON (October 20, 2026) – Pending home sales in September decreased by 7.3% month-over-month and 11.3% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Pending Home Sales report . The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract. Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. The West had the largest decrease, followed by the South, Midwest and Northeast. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions. “Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates.” “Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve’s short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out,” Yun said. “However, increasing energy prices and the resulting inflationary pressure are highly uncertain.” “Despite the difficulty of obtaining a mortgage, the limited number of distressed properties is ensuring steady home prices,” Yun added. “Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably.” September 2026 National Pending Home Sales 7.3% decrease month-over-month 11.3% decrease year-over-year September 2026 Regional Pending Home Sales Northeast 4.2% decrease month-over-month 9.4% decrease year-over-year Midwest 6.5% decrease month-over-month 8.7% decrease year-over-year South 8.2% decrease month-over-month 12.0% decrease year-over-year West 9.2% decrease month-over-month 15.0% decrease year-over-year At the local level, pending home sales fell year-over-year even in the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the following 10 markets posted the smallest annual declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com ® Economics: Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (-2.0%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-2.1%) San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont, CA (-3.5%) San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, CA (-4.6%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, NY (-5.6%) Richmond, VA (-5.8%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-5.9%) Pittsburgh, PA (-6.2%) Memphis, TN-MS-AR (-6.3%) San Antonio-New Braunfels, TX (-7.1%) About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes—from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation—visit facts.realtor . # # # *The Pending Home Sales Index is a leading indicator for the housing sector, based on pending sales of existing homes. A sale is listed as pending when the contract has been signed but the transaction has not closed, though the sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing. Pending contracts are good early indicators of upcoming sales closings. However, the amount of time between pending contracts and completed sales is not identical for all home sales. Variations in the length of the process from pending contract to closed sale can be caused by issues such as buyer difficulties with obtaining mortgage financing, home inspection problems, or appraisal issues. The index is based on a sample that covers about 40% of multiple listing service data each month. In developing the model for the index, it was demonstrated that the level of monthly sales-contract activity parallels the level of closed existing-home sales in the following two months. An index of 100 is equal to the average level of contract activity during 2001, which was the first year to be examined. items.title: Apartment List National Rent Report
items.description: Apartment List National Rent Report By: Chris Salviati and Rob Warnock October 28, 2026 Headline Market Update: November 2026 Year-over-year rent growth in the U.S. flipped positive in October for the first time since mid-2023, though just barely. The national median rent currently stands at $1,384, and is now 0.1% greater than it was at this time last year. The vacancy rate is also gradually tightening, as the market transitions out of the soft conditions that have prevailed in recent years. That said, our newest market indicator tracking the concession rate, continues to show signs of softness. Key Stats National Median Rent: $1,384 per month as of October 2026. Year-Over-Year Rent Growth: Rents are up 0.1% compared to October 2025, marking the first time in over three years that year-over-year rent growth is positive. Month-Over-Month Rent Growth: Rents decreased 0.3% in October 2026 as the rental market enters its off-season; this marks the second consecutive monthly decline. Vacancy Rate: The national multifamily vacancy rate sits at 7% as of October 2026, remaining elevated compared to long-run norms, but continuing to decline after peaking earlier this year. Time on Market: Units are taking an average of 36 days to get leased after being listed, a bit longer than is typical for this time of year. Concessions Rate: 32% of multifamily properties nationally are offering concessions on new leases valued at one month of free rent or greater in October. The concessions rate remains four percentage points higher than at this time last year. Year-over-year rent growth flips positive for first time in over three years For years, the U.S. rental market has been experiencing a prolonged period of sluggishness, as a large wave of multifamily construction had been driving soft pricing and occupancy. However, we’re now at the tail end of that construction boom, and the market has been gradually moving toward more balanced conditions. This month’s data marks a significant milestone in that transition, as year-over-year rent growth flipped positive for the first time in over three years. Following a period of booming rent growth in 2021 and 2022, prices began to cool rapidly, and by June 2023, the national median rent was declining on a year-over-year basis. Full year rent growth was negative for three consecutive years, with prices nationally dipping by -0.8 percent in 2023, by -0.5 percent in 2024, and by -1.2 percent in 2026. Year-over-year rent growth bottomed out at -1.6 percent in April 2026, but over the past six months it has rebounded rapidly as healthy renter demand has filled vacant units and allowed property owners and operators to regain some pricing leverage. Despite the bounceback, rents are still essentially flat compared to one year ago, and are still declining in inflation-adjusted terms. Nonetheless, it’s a significant milestone for the rental market that year-over-year rent growth has now flipped positive. Even as year-year-over rent growth continues to rise, month-over-month rent growth remained negative in October, as the market experiences its typical off-season pricing dip. Fewer renters tend to move in the fall in winter months, and so property owners offer modest discounts to attract demand and fill vacant units at this time of year. But compared to recent years, this year’s fall cooldown has been significantly more subdued. Rents fell by just 0.3 percent in October compared to September; in October of last year, the month-over-month decline was nearly three times as sharp at -0.8 percent. In fact this month’s decline was even slightly more modest than the 2017 to 2019 average (-0.4 percent), a period when the national rental market was in a well-balanced state. In dollar terms, the national median monthly rent now stands at $1,384, up just $1 compared to October 2025. Prices peaked in mid-2022, and have since fallen from that peak by a total of 4 percent, or $58 per month. The national median rent also recently hit a notable milestone – years of modest declines have now offset the rapid price growth that preceded it such that prices are converging back to their long run trend. After oscillating between alternating hot and cool spells throughout the 2020s, the national median rent today is roughly where it would have been if rents had continued to grow at a slow and steady pace of +2.5 percent annually, the average rent growth from 2017 to 2019. This convergence has occurred just as rent growth appears set to stabilize back to something resembling that late-2010s average. Our new concessions rate indicator continues to show some softness This month, in an effort to continue providing actionable, real-time data on the rental market, the Apartment List Economics Team is adding a new dataset to our suite of market indicators: concession rates. Properties that are struggling with occupancy often employ concessions as a strategy for securing new leases. Concessions can take many forms, including discounted rents, cash back offers, gift cards, or free amenities. Such concessions are not factored into our rent estimates, and so tracking them separately provides additional nuance on market conditions. Our published concession rate represents the share of properties offering any discount whose total value is equal to one free month of rent or greater. As of October, 32 percent of all properties are offering concessions valued at one month of free rent or greater. The current concession rate is four percentage points higher than this time last year, when 28 percent of properties were offering such discounts. The concession rate has also ticked up very slightly over the past two months as we enter the off-season. items.title: Hidden Costs of Homeownership Top $16.6K a Year as Insurance Climbs
items.description: Hidden Costs of Homeownership Top $16.6K a Year as Insurance Climbs The typical U.S. homeowner pays $16,566 a year, about $1,380 a month, for maintenance, property taxes and insurance on top of a mortgage payment. Written by Kara Ng on October 22, 2026 The typical U.S. homeowner pays $16,566 a year, about $1,380 a month, for maintenance, property taxes and insurance on top of a mortgage payment, a new Zillow and Thumbtack analysis finds. That total is up 3% in the past year. Insurance premiums are up 54% in five years, outpacing maintenance (32%) and property taxes (19%). In Houston, Phoenix, Denver and Nashville, homeowners now pay more for insurance than for property taxes. Hidden costs range from $14,187 a year in Phoenix to $25,111 in New York. Maintenance is the largest cost in every metro analyzed. Many households focus on winning the home and underestimate what it costs to live in it, and those recurring costs add to the affordability challenge of homeownership. Here is how the hidden costs break down for the typical U.S. homeowner: Maintenance: $11,171 a year, about two-thirds of the total Property taxes: $3,129 a year (estimated) Homeowners insurance: $2,266 a year (estimated) Insurance is the fastest-rising cost Over the past five years, insurance premiums have risen 54%, compared with 32% for maintenance and 19% for property taxes. That shift is changing the math in some of the country's biggest metro areas. In Houston, Phoenix, Denver and Nashville, the typical homeowner now pays more each year for insurance than for property taxes. Premiums are up at least 50% over five years in 19 of the 30 metros analyzed. The steepest increases are in Dallas (75%), Tampa (71%), Denver (70%) and Houston (69%). Miami homeowners pay the most for insurance at nearly $5,000 a year, up 62% in five years. Six metros now top $3,000 a year: Miami, Dallas, Houston, Tampa, Orlando and Denver. Maintenance remains the largest cost Maintenance is the largest hidden cost in every metro analyzed, and it tops $12K in Seattle ($12,594) and Boston ($12,486). Los Angeles saw the sharpest year-over-year jump in maintenance costs, at 27%. The increase was primarily driven by ongoing wildfire recovery efforts, heightened demand for residential services and elevated labor costs. Hidden costs are highest in expensive coastal metros Total hidden costs are highest in New York ($25,111), San Francisco ($24,383), Boston ($22,096), and Seattle ($21,354). Even in Phoenix, the least costly metro analyzed, they run $14,187 a year. Over five years, hidden costs rose the most in Pittsburgh (54.8%), Tampa (44.4%), Miami (42.8%) and Los Angeles (42.5%). New York, where costs are already highest, rose the least, at 13.8%. Methodology Zillow estimated annual property tax and homeowners insurance costs for a typical U.S. homeowner in each of 30 metros, then compared year-over-year and five-year changes. Thumbtack provided estimates for annual home maintenance costs, based on projects requested on Thumbtack and reported directly by the independent service professional or individual customer. The maintenance cost is an unweighted index of yearly home maintenance projects, calculated quarterly using a moving average. items.title: New Home Market Update
items.description: New Home Market Update Zonda tracks 85% of the production new home market across the United States. Given the proprietary database, Zonda is uniquely positioned to capture trends and changes in the new home market. This report showcases the latest housing trends in the new home market for September 2026. October 22, 2026 – 5 min read Table of Content: Pressure builds on the new home market September brought little relief for the new home market: although overall sales rose a modest 1.7% month-over-month, they remained 4.6% below where they stood this time last year. The market showed widespread underperformance despite nearly 40% of builders cutting prices in September, up from 30% in August. Zonda's September builder sentiment survey reinforced the weakness, with 84% of builders reporting slower-than-expected demand, including 60% who said the slowdown was causing concern. Mortgage rates have only added to the pressure, crossing the 7% threshold in late September and climbing further into October. Alongside broader economic uncertainty, higher borrowing costs are making it harder for builders to maintain sales without putting additional pressure on margins. Even when the numbers work, though, buyers may hesitate to make such a significant financial commitment if they're uncertain about their jobs or the broader economy. “The silver lining we’re seeing in the market today is at the high end,” said Ali Wolf, chief economist for Zonda and NewHomeSource. “Prices in the entry-level and move-up/move-down segments declined in September but rose in the high-end market. That doesn’t mean high-end sales are easy. Rather, it reflects that buyers with greater wealth are better positioned to navigate today’s challenging market.” New home sales fell further behind last year Zonda's new home sales metric counts the number of new home contract sales each month and accounts for both cancellations and seasonality. This metric shows there were 690,215 new homes sold in September on a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. This was a gain of 1.7% from last month and a drop of 4.6% from a year ago. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, 54,334 homes were sold, 4.6% lower than last year and 3.0% above the same month in 2019. Incentives remain a key feature of the new home market, helping to sustain sales activity amid ongoing affordability pressures. In September, 63% of new home communities offered incentives on to-be-built homes and 82% on quick move-in supply. Note, these are only publicly available incentives so will underrepresent overall usage. Pending sales were also subdued Zonda's New Home Pending Sales Index (PSI) was created to help account for fluctuations in supply by combining both total sales volume with the average sales rate per month per community. The September PSI came in at 132.0, representing a 6.0% decline from the same month last year. The index is currently 24.2% below cycle highs. On a month-over-month basis, seasonally adjusted new home sales increased 3.4%. The markets that posted the best numbers relative to last year were Baltimore (+30.3%), New York (+23.2%), and Tampa (+9.7%). Baltimore was up compared to last year and grew 20.4% month-over-month. Inversely, the metros that performed the worst year-over-year were Denver (-40.5%), Washington, DC (-29.0%), and Las Vegas (-17.0%). On a monthly basis, Baltimore, Riverside/San Bernardino, and Los Angeles/OC were the best performing markets. Underperforming markets were widespread In order to add further context to sales, Zonda created the Zonda Market Ranking (ZMR). The ZMR accounts for both sales pace and volume, is seasonally adjusted, and is taken as a percentage relative to a baseline market average. Based on the percentage above or below baseline, markets are bucketed into performance groups ranging from significantly underperforming to significantly overperforming relative to historical activity. The map below shows a snapshot of top production markets by region. Zonda also offers the ZMR for entry-level, move-up/move-down, and high-end markets. Subscribers of the National Outlook report can access all top markets and the tiered breakdown in Zonda’s portal. Non-subscribers can access the tiered maps for the select 10 markets by clicking below. Get ZMR Maps The National ZMR index came in at 95.8 in September, which continued to indicate an average market. Zonda’s snapshot markets were split between 0% overperforming, 30% average, and 70% underperforming. Among Zonda’s top 55 major markets, 14% were overperforming , 33% were average , and 53% were underperforming . Importantly, the ZMR does not account for what it takes to sell a home. For example, securing a sale might still feel difficult in a significantly overperforming market, but if the incentives offered result in a sale, we count the sale. More builders turned to price cuts National home prices increased 2.0% year-over-year for high-end homes to $946,207. Prices fell 2.6% for entry-level to $316,246 and 0.8% for move-up to $513,294. The increase among higher-priced homes reflects a concentration of new communities opening at premium price points, along with larger homesites, bigger floor plans, and more desirable locations. Meanwhile, modest price declines in the entry-level and move-up segments suggest builders continue to prioritize affordability through incentives, product right-sizing, and more competitive pricing in response to softer buyer demand. Supplementing our data with a survey Zonda conducts monthly, 38% of builders lowered prices in September month-over-month, 52% held prices flat, and 10% raised prices. In August, for comparison, 30% of builders lowered prices, 63% held prices flat, and 7% increased prices. Community count up 6.5% from last year There are currently 18,143 actively selling communities tracked by Zonda, up 6.5% year-over-year. On a month-over-month basis, the national figure grew 0.8%. Total community count is 6.0% below the same month in 2019.

items.title: Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3
items.description: Economic Coverage , Homeownership Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3 By Hannah Jones Oct 28, 2026 2026 Q3 Homeownership and Housing Vacancy Key Takeaways Homeownership rate holds steady. The U.S. homeownership rate was 65.5% in Q3 2026, statistically unchanged from both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). The rate continues to plateau in a narrow low-to-mid-65% band, with affordability pressures and limited supply showing little sign of easing their grip on the market. Homeowner vacancy remains low and steady. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3, virtually unchanged from both the prior quarter and a year earlier. Rental vacancy reaches its highest level in over a decade. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6%, up both quarter-over-quarter (7.3%) and year-over-year (7.1%), its highest level since 2014. Renting remains a critical pressure valve, though conditions vary by geography. With a national rental vacancy rate of 7.6%, rental markets continue to offer more flexibility for households unable to buy. Principal cities (8.8%) remain looser than suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%), which were statistically similar to each other. The South leads in vacancy levels, while the Northeast and West saw the clearest year-over-year shifts. The South posted the highest rental vacancy rate (9.2%) and homeowner vacancy rate (1.5%) of any region, though neither was statistically different from a year ago. Rental vacancy rose significantly in the Northeast (5.0% to 6.2%) and the West (6.0% to 6.7%). Ownership slipped among 35-to-44-year-olds, while older households gained. Homeownership among 35-to-44-year-olds fell from 61.1% to 60.1% year-over-year. Households under 35 remain the lowest at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Meanwhile, 65+ homeownership rose from 77.9% to 79.1%. Racial ownership gaps remain entrenched. Homeownership among Black households fell from 45.7% to 44.4% year-over-year, while White homeownership rose from 74.0% to 75.1%. All other groups did not see statistically significant shifts. What happened this quarter The U.S. homeownership rate held at 65.5% in the third quarter of 2026, statistically unchanged compared with both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). While the rate remains within the narrow low-to-mid-65% range that has characterized the market in recent years, it continues to run well below the 2020 pandemic-era peak. Mortgage rates pushed back above 7% in late September for the first time in more than a year, which could weigh on would-be buyers heading into the fourth quarter. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3 2026, virtually the same as the previous quarter and the previous year. While homeowner vacancy remains below pre-pandemic norms, the recent pick up in inventory could mean vacancy drifts higher if demand is not sufficient to absorb supply. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6% in the third quarter, higher than both the previous quarter (7.3%) and the previous year (7.1%). With mortgage rates moving back above 7%, renting continues to stand out as a more affordable alternative to homeownership. However, climbing rental vacancy suggests that units are sitting empty as affordability pressure may discourage household formation. Vacancy was highest in principal cities (8.8%). Suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%) were lower and not statistically different from each other. Regional differences remain pronounced . The South recorded the highest rental vacancy rate at 9.2%, followed by the Midwest (7.1%), the West (6.7%), and the Northeast (6.2%). The Midwest was higher than the Northeast and statistically similar to the West, while the Northeast and West were not statistically different from each other. Of the four regions, only the Northeast (up from 5.0%) and West (up from 6.0%) saw a statistically significant year-over-year increase in rental vacancy. Rental vacancy has stalled in the South as the wave of supply has subsided . The post-pandemic construction boom flooded these markets with new supply, but as multifamily construction has slowed, vacancy growth has stalled. On the ownership side, the South again led with the highest homeowner vacancy rate at 1.5%, while the other three regions saw vacancy between 0.9% and 1.1%. The Midwest continues to stand out for its high homeownership rate, reaching 69.5% in Q3 2026, though not statistically different from a year earlier, and remains well above the South (67.2%), Northeast (62.9%), and West (60.6%). Different outcomes by race/ethnicity Homeownership rates by race and ethnicity were mixed year over year. In the third quarter, the rate for non-Hispanic White householders rose to 75.1% from 74.0%, while the rate for Asian, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander householders was statistically unchanged at 62.3%. The rate for Black householders fell to 44.4% from 45.7%, and the rate for Hispanic householders was statistically unchanged at 48.1%. The gap between the highest and lowest rates remains more than 30 percentage points, underscoring the persistence of structural barriers to ownership. Different outcomes by age Ownership among younger households remains low, while older householders saw improvement. Homeownership among those under 35 was the lowest of any age group at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Homeownership among households aged 35 to 44 fell from 61.1% in Q3 of 2025 to 60.1% in Q3 of 2026. Ownership in the 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 cohorts held steady at 70.4% and 75.4%, respectively, while the 65+ group saw a 1.2 percentage point improvement to 79.1%. Ample starter-home inventory is crucial for young homeownership, and availability varies significantly across the country .

This is 1.0 percent (±0.9 percent) below the August 2026 estimate of 481,000, and is 2.3 percent (±4.0 percent)* below the September 2025 estimate of 487,000. This represents a supply of 8.4 months at the current sales rate. The months' supply is 1.2 percent (±14.7 percent)* below the August 2026 estimate of 8.5 months, and is 2.4 percent (±14.1 percent)* above the September 2025 estimate of 8.2 months. Sales Price The median sales price of new houses sold in September 2026 was $400,400. This is 3.9 percent (±6.2 percent)* above the August 2026 price of $385,400, and is 3.9 percent (±8.9 percent)* below the September 2025 price of $416,800. The average sales price of new houses sold in September 2026 was $472,800. This is 0.4 percent (±6.1 percent)* above the August 2026 price of $470,800, and is 6.7 percent (±6.6 percent) below the September 2025 price of $506,800. items.title: Mortgage Rates
items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 10/29/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.24% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.60% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline Further to 7.24% The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.24% as of October 29, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.32%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.17%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.60%, down from last week when it averaged 6.68%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.41%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained .
